one: How a team organises branches. Trunk-based means short-lived branches merged to main daily; GitFlow keeps long-lived develop/release branches.
an: Trunk-based is everyone adding small bricks to one wall every day. GitFlow is each team building a whole section elsewhere and trying to fit it in at the end.
how: Trunk-based: branches live hours to a couple of days, main is always deployable, unfinished features hide behind feature flags.
GitFlow: develop, release/*, hotfix/*. Suits shipped software with versions (mobile apps, libraries, on-prem).
The longer a branch lives, the more painful the merge and the later you discover integration bugs.
why: DORA research links trunk-based development to higher delivery performance. Its measurable signs: three or fewer active branches, branches merged to trunk at least once a day, and no code freezes. Leads choose the workflow and enforce it with branch rules.
trade: Trunk-based needs good CI, tests and flags. Without them, main breaks often.

myth.m: Long feature branches are safer because main stays clean.
myth.r: They move risk to a giant merge at the end. Small merges keep risk small and continuous.

q.s: A 3-week feature branch has 140 merge conflicts with main. What practice prevents this next time?
o: Longer code freezes
Merging small slices to main daily behind a feature flag
Fewer reviewers
Squashing commits
q.e: Integrate continuously. Flags decouple merging code from releasing the feature.

more: Short-lived feature branches and PR size
Merge vs rebase vs squash, and keeping history readable
lab: For one week, keep every branch under one day old. Hide unfinished work behind a simple flag. Note what was hard.
Practise git rebase main on a branch with conflicts and git log --oneline --graph to read history.
docs: Martin Fowler: Patterns for managing source code branches

plain:
A branching strategy is the team's agreement on how code gets from a developer to the main branch. In trunk-based development, branches are tiny and merged into main at least daily. In GitFlow, there are long-lived branches like develop and release.

The longer a branch lives away from main, the more painful and risky it is to merge.
bridge: If you have spent a whole afternoon fixing merge conflicts after a two-week feature branch, you have felt the problem trunk-based development solves.

walk.title: Shipping a big feature in small merges
steps: Feature: a new checkout flow, about two weeks of work.
Day 1: merge a feature flag newCheckout (off) and an empty page behind it.
Days 2–9: merge small PRs every day: the cart summary, the address form, the payment step. Users see nothing because the flag is off.
Day 10: turn the flag on for the team only. Fix what they find.
Day 12: turn it on for 10% of users, then everyone. No giant merge, no “merge day” fear.

terms: The main branch that is always deployable.
A branch for one piece of work.
Two changes touching the same lines; a human must decide.
A switch that hides unfinished code from users.
insights: Watch branch age and PR size. A PR of a few hundred lines gets a real review; a 2,000-line PR usually gets a quick “LGTM”.
“Main is green” is a team habit: whoever breaks main reverts or fixes it first, before any other work.
GitFlow is a release-process choice, not a quality choice. Use it only when customers really run several versions of your software.

prod.summary: In production teams, branching is enforced by tooling, not by a wiki page: protected main, required CI checks, required reviews, and often a merge queue. Seniors watch branch age and PR size, because those two numbers predict merge pain and review quality better than any branching diagram.
checklist: main is protected: no direct pushes, required status checks, at least one approving review, force-push disabled.
Branches older than 2–3 days are visible somewhere (a bot comment or a dashboard) and someone asks why.
Unfinished work is merged behind a feature flag that defaults to off, not kept on a long branch.
Large changes are split into stacked or sequential PRs of a few hundred lines that can be reviewed in one sitting.
If many people merge per hour, a merge queue tests each PR on top of the latest main, so two green PRs cannot combine into a red main.
Release branches exist only where versions are really shipped (mobile apps, libraries, on-prem). Fixes go to main first, then are cherry-picked to the release branch.
The team has agreed on one merge style (squash, rebase or merge commit) so history is readable and git revert of one PR is one command.
numbers: DORA's trunk-based development capability: three or fewer active branches, and branches merged to trunk at least once a day.
GitHub “Require branches to be up to date before merging” forces a re-run of CI after every other merge; with many PRs a day this becomes a queue of re-runs, which is the problem merge queues solve.
failures: Release day: a 3-week branch has hundreds of conflicts and the merge takes a full day; bugs appear in code nobody changed.
The branch drifted from main, so integration bugs were hidden until the end. Fix: merge small slices daily behind a flag; rebase or merge main into any branch that must live longer, every day.
Two PRs are green on their own, both merge, and main goes red.
Each PR was tested against an old main, not against the other change (a “semantic conflict”: no text conflict, but broken together). Fix: require up-to-date branches or use a merge queue.
A hotfix is shipped from a release branch, and the same bug comes back in the next release.
The fix was never applied to main. Fix: always merge to main first and cherry-pick to the release branch, never the other way round.
! [rejected] feature -> feature (non-fast-forward) after a rebase, then a teammate's commits disappear.
Someone used git push --force on a shared branch and overwrote work. Fix: use --force-with-lease, which refuses if the remote has commits you have not seen.

code.title: A short-lived branch, kept close to main
code.src:
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
git switch -c feat/checkout-address-form

# ...small change, behind a flag that is off by default...
git commit -am "feat(checkout): address form behind newCheckout flag"

# Before opening the PR (and every morning if it lives longer):
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

# Safe force-push: fails if someone else pushed to this branch
git push --force-with-lease -u origin feat/checkout-address-form

# After merge: delete the branch so it cannot drift
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
git branch -d feat/checkout-address-form
code.note: --force-with-lease is the line that matters: it rewrites your own branch after a rebase, but refuses to overwrite commits you have not fetched.

qs.s: Your team merges about 40 PRs a day. Twice this week, two PRs that were each green merged one after the other and broke main. What fixes this at the root?
o: A merge queue that tests each PR on top of main plus the PRs ahead of it
Requiring two reviewers instead of one
Switching to GitFlow with a develop branch
Running CI only after merge, on main
qs.e: The PRs had no text conflict but broke together. Only testing the combined result catches that. More reviewers rarely spot it, and GitFlow just moves the same break to develop.

qs.s: A mobile team ships to the App Store every two weeks and must support version 5.2 while 5.3 is in review. Which setup fits best?
o: Pure trunk-based, deploy every commit to the store
One long-lived branch per developer
Trunk-based development on main, plus a short release branch cut per store version for fixes only
No branches; tag commits and patch tags directly
qs.e: Store review and installed versions mean real shipped versions exist, so a release branch for fixes is reasonable. Daily work still integrates on main. Developer branches recreate the merge-hell problem.

qs.s: A developer must build a feature that takes 3 weeks and touches the payment page. Leadership wants main deployable every day. What do you suggest?
o: Keep a feature branch and merge main into it weekly
Freeze the payment page for 3 weeks
Write the whole feature in a separate repository
Merge small PRs daily with the new code behind a flag that is off in production
qs.e: Flags let incomplete code live on main without users seeing it, so integration happens daily. A long branch, even with weekly syncs, still delays integration and review.

qs.s: Your team merges PRs with merge commits. PR #482 (12 commits) broke production. You must undo it on protected main right now. Read the history. Which command is correct?

code.title: git log --oneline --graph -6
code.src:
*   9e1f2ab (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Merge pull request #482 from acme/feat/coupon-v2
|\
| * 51c0d9e fix lint
| * 0c47e1a apply coupon at checkout
| * ...     (9 more commits)
|/
*   7a3b001 Merge pull request #481 from acme/fix/tax-rounding

o: git reset --hard 7a3b001 && git push --force
git revert 51c0d9e
git revert -m 1 9e1f2ab, then push it as a normal PR
git revert HEAD~12..HEAD
qs.e: Reverting the merge commit with -m 1 (keep the first parent, which is main) creates one new commit that removes the whole PR, without rewriting history. reset --hard plus force-push rewrites shared history and is blocked on a protected branch anyway. Reverting 51c0d9e only undoes the lint fix. Note: if you later want to re-merge the same branch, you must revert the revert first.

qs.s: A 1,800-line PR was approved in 6 minutes with “LGTM” and caused an incident. The lead wants better reviews. Which change helps most?
o: Split work into small, stacked PRs (a few hundred lines each) that merge daily behind a flag
Require 3 approvals instead of 1
Make the author write a longer PR description
Only allow seniors to approve
qs.e: Big diffs get skimmed: reviewers cannot hold 1,800 lines in their head, so more approvers just means more people skimming. Small PRs get real review and also merge sooner, which reduces drift from main.

qs.s: Ana and Ben both push to feat/search. Ben pushed a commit 10 minutes ago. Ana now runs the commands below. What happens to Ben's commit?

code.title: Ana's terminal
code.src:
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
git push --force-with-lease origin feat/search

o: The push is rejected, because the remote has a commit Ana does not have locally
The push succeeds and Ben's commit is lost: git fetch updated origin/feat/search, so the lease check passes
Git merges Ben's commit into Ana's branch automatically
The push succeeds and GitHub keeps Ben's commit on a backup branch
qs.e: --force-with-lease only checks that the remote still matches your remote-tracking ref. The fetch moved that ref to include Ben's commit, so the lease is satisfied even though Ana's local branch never contained it. Add --force-if-includes (Git 2.30+), which also checks that the remote tip is in your local history, or rebase with git pull --rebase first. Better still: do not share a branch you rebase.

qs.s: Your team runs one SaaS web app with a single production version and deploys 5 times a day. A new hire proposes GitFlow (develop, release/*, hotfix/*) because “it is the industry standard”. What is your answer?
o: Adopt it: more branches mean more safety
Adopt it, but only for the backend
Use GitFlow, but merge develop into main daily
Stay trunk-based: release branches only pay off when several versions must be supported at the same time, which a single-version SaaS never needs
qs.e: GitFlow's extra branches exist to stabilise and patch shipped versions. With one live version and many deploys a day, they only add merges and delay integration. Merging develop daily into main is trunk-based development with an extra hop.

interview.q: Your team uses long-lived feature branches and “merge week” is painful. How would you move them to trunk-based development?
answer: Start with the reasons for long branches: fear of breaking main, slow CI, unfinished features. Fix those first, or people will go back.
Make CI fast (under ~10 minutes) and required, and protect main, so merging often is safe.
Introduce feature flags so unfinished work can merge while hidden; give each flag an owner and removal date.
Set a measurable target (DORA: branches merged at least daily, three or fewer active branches) and show branch age on a dashboard.
Migrate gradually: one team or service first, then share the results. Keep release branches only where real versions ship (mobile, libraries).
followups: How do you handle a database migration that takes several PRs?
What do you do when CI is too slow to merge daily?

interview.q: Squash, rebase, or merge commits: which merge style would you choose for a team, and why?
answer: Squash: one commit per PR on main; easy to read and to revert with a plain git revert. You lose the individual commits on main (they stay in the PR).
Rebase: linear history with every commit; good if the team writes clean, atomic commits, noisy otherwise.
Merge commits: keep the exact branch history; reverting needs -m 1; the graph gets busy with many PRs.
The choice matters less than consistency: one style, enforced in repository settings.
Tie it to tooling: conventional commit messages on squash commits can drive changelogs and semver releases.
followups: How do you revert a merge commit, and what happens when you re-merge the same branch later?
How do stacked PRs work with squash merges?

interview.q: Two PRs were green, merged, and main went red. Explain how that is possible and how you would stop it at scale.
answer: Each PR was tested against an older main. They had no text conflict but a semantic one (for example one renamed a function, the other added a call to the old name).
Option 1: require branches to be up to date before merge. Correct, but at high PR volume everyone keeps rebasing and re-running CI.
Option 2: a merge queue. It tests each PR on top of main plus the PRs ahead of it, and merges only if that combination is green.
Keep main CI as a final safety net, with fast auto-revert or a clear owner when it goes red.
Trade-off: a queue adds some wait time and needs CI to run on the queue's temporary branches.
followups: What happens in a merge queue when one PR in a batch fails?
How would you keep queue wait time low?

diagrams.src:

codeCheck.detail: Ran the snippet against a bare origin with a teammate commit on main: rebase, --force-with-lease push and branch cleanup all worked; the lease refused a push over an unfetched teammate commit. Practice: reproduced qs5 (fetch then lease silently drops Ben's commit, --force-if-includes rejects it) and qs3 (revert -m 1 restores the pre-PR tree).

videos.t: 3 Git Workflows Every Developer Should Know (And When to Use Each)
videos.why: Three Git workflows and when each one fits.

one: Every push automatically builds the code and runs checks (types, lint, tests) so problems are caught within minutes.
an: A spell-checker that reads every page as you write it, not a proofreader who sees the book once it is printed.
how: A pipeline (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI) runs on each push/PR: install → lint → typecheck → unit tests → build → integration tests → build image.
Branch protection blocks merging until checks pass and a review approves.
Speed is a feature: cache dependencies, parallelise test shards, run the slow suites only where needed. A 40-minute CI changes how people work, for the worse.
why: It keeps main always working and gives fast feedback, which is the foundation for deploying often.
trade: Flaky tests destroy trust: people start re-running until green and ignoring real failures. Quarantine and fix them quickly.

myth.r: CI is the practice of integrating to main frequently with automated verification. The YAML is the tool.

q.s: Your team re-runs failed CI jobs until they pass about once a day. What is the real risk?
o: Higher CI bill only
Real failures get dismissed as flakiness and reach production
Slower laptops
Merge conflicts
q.e: Flakiness trains people to ignore red. Track flaky tests, quarantine them, and fix them as priority work.

more: Required status checks and merge queues
lab: Write a GitHub Actions workflow: install with cache, lint, typecheck, unit tests, build. Make it a required check on main.
Add a Postgres service container and run integration tests against it.
Measure the run time, then cut it in half (caching, parallel jobs).

plain: Continuous integration means: every time someone pushes code, an automatic pipeline builds it and runs checks (types, lint, tests). If anything fails, the team knows within minutes, before the code reaches main.
bridge: The green checkmark or red cross on your GitHub pull requests comes from CI, usually GitHub Actions running a YAML file in .github/workflows.

walk.title: What runs when you open a pull request
steps: You push a branch and open a PR.
GitHub Actions starts a fresh machine, checks out your code, and restores the dependency cache.
It runs npm ci, then lint, then tsc --noEmit, then unit tests, then the build.
A second job starts a Postgres container and runs integration tests against it.
All green: the PR can be merged (branch protection requires it). One red: merge is blocked and the log shows which step failed.

terms: The list of automated steps CI runs.
A group of steps on one machine / one command.
Rules like “CI must pass before merge”.
A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change.
insights: Put the fastest checks first (lint, types). Most mistakes then fail in the first minute, not after a 10-minute test run.
Make a check required only if the team trusts it. A required check that is often red for no reason gets bypassed, and then it protects nothing.
CI time only grows unless someone owns it. Look at the slowest runs every few weeks and cut the worst step.

prod.summary: Production CI is a fast, trusted gate: it runs on every PR, it is required before merge, and its result is believed. Seniors watch three things: total time to green (aim for under ~10 minutes), flaky-test rate, and whether CI tests the same thing that ships (same Node version, same lockfile, same Dockerfile).
checklist: Dependencies install with npm ci (or pnpm install --frozen-lockfile) and are cached by lockfile hash.
The Node version in CI comes from one place (.nvmrc or engines) and matches production.
Every job has timeout-minutes; the default is 6 hours, so a hung test can burn a runner all morning.
concurrency with cancel-in-progress: true on PR workflows, so pushing 5 commits does not run 5 pipelines.
Workflow permissions are set to the minimum (often contents: read); third-party actions are pinned to a full commit SHA.
Required checks are never skipped by workflow-level paths filters: a skipped workflow stays “Pending” and blocks the PR. Skip inside the job with if: instead.
Integration tests use real service containers (Postgres, Redis) with health checks, not mocks only.
Flaky tests are tracked; a test that fails without code changes is quarantined within a day and has an owner.
numbers: GitHub Actions: a job on a GitHub-hosted runner can run for at most 6 hours.
GitHub Actions cache: 10 GB per repository by default (admins can raise it); entries not used for 7 days are removed.
GitHub Actions: a matrix can generate at most 256 jobs per workflow run.
failures: npm error `npm ci` can only install packages when your package.json and package-lock.json are in sync
Someone changed package.json without committing the updated lockfile. Fix: run npm install locally, commit the lockfile. This error is CI doing its job.
Integration tests fail randomly with ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432.
Tests start before Postgres is ready. Fix: add a health check (pg_isready) to the service container so the job waits.
CI takes 35 minutes; developers stack PRs and merge without waiting.
No caching and everything runs serially. Fix: cache by lockfile hash, split lint/typecheck/test into parallel jobs, shard the slow test suite, and run e2e only on affected paths.
A docs-only PR is stuck on “Expected — Waiting for status to be reported”.
The required workflow has a paths: filter, so it never ran and never reported. Fix: let the workflow always run and skip work with a job-level if:; a job skipped by a condition reports success.
The same commit passes on re-run. The team re-runs “until green” several times a day.
Flaky tests (timing, shared state, test order). Fix: record flaky failures, quarantine the test, fix the root cause; never normalise blind re-runs.

code.title: A fast, safe PR workflow (GitHub Actions)
code.src:
name: ci
on: [pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test }
        ports: ["5432:5432"]
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres"
          --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with: { persist-credentials: false }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint && npx tsc --noEmit
      - run: npm test
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:test@localhost:5432/postgres
code.note: --health-cmd makes the job wait until Postgres accepts connections; without it you get random ECONNREFUSED failures. persist-credentials: false stops the token from staying on disk for later steps. Third-party actions should be pinned to a full commit SHA; the actions/* majors here are current as of 2026 (checkout v7, setup-node v7).

qs.s: A developer pushes 6 commits to a PR in 10 minutes. Each push starts a 12-minute workflow. Runners are queued and other teams wait. Best fix?
o: Buy more runners
Run CI only once a day
Add concurrency with cancel-in-progress: true for PR workflows
Ask developers to push less often
qs.e: Only the latest commit matters for a PR. Cancelling older runs frees runners instantly. More runners just pay for wasted work.

qs.s: CI log: tests pass, but production crashes with SyntaxError on a new JS feature. CI uses node-version: 24, the production image is node:20-alpine. What is the lesson?
o: Alpine images are unsafe
CI must use the same runtime as production, read from one shared source
Syntax errors cannot be caught by CI
Pin the TypeScript version
qs.e: CI proved the code works on Node 24, not on Node 20. Read the version from .nvmrc in both CI and the Dockerfile, or run tests inside the production image.

qs.s: Your workflow uses some-org/deploy-action@main and has permissions: write-all. A security review flags it. What is the main risk?
o: If that action's main branch is compromised, attacker code runs with write access to your repo and secrets
The action may become slower
GitHub will deprecate @main references
It uses more cache storage
qs.e: A moving reference runs whatever is pushed next. Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA and give the workflow the least permissions it needs.

qs.s: Branch protection on main requires the check test. A PR changes only README.md. What happens?

code.title: .github/workflows/api.yml
code.src:
name: api
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["api/**"]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: npm ci && npm test
        working-directory: api

o: The check is skipped and counts as passed
The PR cannot be merged: the workflow never runs, so test stays “Expected — Waiting for status to be reported”
GitHub runs the workflow anyway because the check is required
The PR merges, but main CI runs the tests afterwards
qs.e: A workflow skipped by a paths filter reports nothing, and the required check waits forever. GitHub's own advice: do not path-filter required workflows. Run the workflow always and use a job-level if: (for example from a changed-files step); a job skipped by a condition reports success.

qs.s: Read the CI log. What is the most likely cause?

code.title: CI log
code.src:
✓ src/cart.test.ts (14 tests)
 ✗ src/checkout.test.ts > applies coupon
   AssertionError: expected 81 to be 90

# Developer, locally:
$ npx vitest run src/checkout.test.ts
 ✓ src/checkout.test.ts (9 tests)

# Both test files use the same Postgres database from DATABASE_URL.

o: The CI runner has a slower CPU
Vitest randomly drops tests
Floating-point rounding differs between machines
Shared state: cart.test.ts leaves data (for example a coupon row) in the shared database, which changes checkout.test.ts
qs.e: Passes alone, fails in the full run, same commit: that is test-order or shared-state leakage. 90 → 81 is exactly an extra 10% discount. Give each test (or file) its own data: a transaction rolled back after each test, unique IDs, or a schema per worker. A slow CPU causes timeouts, not wrong totals.

qs.s: A serial pipeline: install 2 min, lint 2 min, typecheck 3 min, unit tests 8 min, build 4 min (19 min). You split it into parallel jobs, and each job repeats the 2-minute install: (lint + typecheck), (unit tests in 4 equal shards), (build). Roughly what is the new wall-clock time?
o: About 7 minutes
About 4 minutes
About 19 minutes
About 10 minutes
qs.e: Parallel jobs finish when the slowest one finishes. lint+typecheck: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7. Each test shard: 2 + 8/4 = 4. build: 2 + 4 = 6. The longest is 7 minutes. The next speed-up is not more test shards, it is the lint/typecheck job (or a faster install cache).

qs.s: To give fork PRs a preview deploy, a workflow uses on: pull_request_target (which has access to secrets), checks out github.event.pull_request.head.sha and runs npm ci && npm run build. What is the problem?
o: Fork PRs cannot trigger pull_request_target
It only wastes runner minutes
The fork author controls package.json scripts and build code, so their code runs with your secrets and a write token (a “pwn request”)
npm ci ignores scripts in CI
qs.e: pull_request_target runs in the context of your repository, with secrets. Running untrusted code there gives it those secrets. actions/checkout@v7 now refuses this checkout by default unless you set allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true. Safe pattern: build fork code in an unprivileged pull_request run, then deploy its artifact from a separate trusted workflow.

interview.q: Our CI takes 40 minutes and is flaky. You have one quarter. What do you do?
answer: Measure first: per-job and per-step timings, queue time vs run time, and a list of tests that failed then passed on the same commit.
Quick wins: dependency cache keyed by lockfile, cancel-in-progress on PRs, parallel jobs for lint/typecheck/test/build, test sharding.
Run expensive suites (e2e) on affected paths or in the merge queue, not on every push, but keep a required fast gate.
Flakes: quarantine within a day with an owner, fix the common causes (shared DB state, real time and sleeps, test order, network calls).
Set a target and track it weekly: for example p50 under 10 minutes, flaky rate under 1% of runs.
followups: How do you stop quarantined tests from staying quarantined forever?
When are self-hosted or larger runners worth it?

interview.q: How do you secure a GitHub Actions setup for a company repository?
answer: Least privilege: default permissions: contents: read, grant more per job only where needed.
Pin third-party actions to full commit SHAs and update them with Dependabot or Renovate.
Never run untrusted fork code with secrets: avoid pull_request_target plus PR checkout; pass inputs to scripts through env, not ${{ }} inside run, to prevent script injection.
Use OIDC for cloud access instead of stored keys, and put production secrets behind a protected environment with reviewers.
Be careful with caches in privileged workflows (cache poisoning), and keep self-hosted runners away from public repos.
followups: What is script injection in a workflow, with an example?
Why pin to a SHA rather than a tag like v7?

interview.q: What should CI test for a typical TypeScript web service, and what should it not try to test?
answer: Fast layer on every push: lint, tsc --noEmit, unit tests.
Integration tests against real dependencies in containers (Postgres, Redis), because mocks hide SQL and driver bugs.
Build the real artifact (the Docker image) in CI, so the thing tested is the thing shipped.
A small set of e2e/contract tests for critical paths (login, checkout), not the whole UI.
Not in CI: tests that need production data or third-party live APIs; those belong in staging checks or monitoring.
Keep the pyramid: many fast tests, few slow ones, and a time budget for the total.
followups: How would you test database migrations in CI?
Where do contract tests between services fit?

log shows failed step"]

one: Delivery: every change that passes CI is releasable at the push of a button. Deployment: it goes to production automatically.
an: A bakery where every loaf that passes inspection goes straight onto the shelf, instead of being stockpiled for a big monthly opening.
how: Build the artifact (image) once, then promote the same artifact through environments: staging → production. Never rebuild per environment.
Automated steps: run migrations, deploy with a safe strategy, run smoke tests, watch metrics, roll back on failure.
Small, frequent deploys mean each one carries little change, so failures are easy to diagnose and revert.
why: DORA research shows that teams which deploy more often also have lower change failure rates and recover faster. Speed and stability go together. It also removes the fear and ceremony around releases.
trade: Needs good tests, observability and fast rollback. Regulated domains may need approval gates, which can still be automated.

myth.r: Bigger batches mean more changes per deploy, harder debugging and scarier rollbacks.

q.s: Why build the Docker image once and promote it, rather than rebuilding for production?
o: Saves disk space
Rebuilding can produce a different artifact than the one you tested
Registries require it
Faster DNS
q.e: Dependencies and base images change. The thing tested should be the thing shipped.

more: Build once, promote the same artifact
lab: Extend your CI so a merge to main builds a Docker image tagged with the git SHA, pushes it, and deploys it to a PaaS or a VM.
Add a smoke test step that curls /healthz after deploy and fails the pipeline if it is not 200.
Practise a rollback: redeploy the previous SHA.

plain:
Continuous delivery means every change that passes CI is ready to release with one click. Continuous deployment goes one step further: it is released automatically.

Releasing small changes often turns out to be safer than releasing big batches rarely, because each release has less that can go wrong and is easy to undo.
bridge: Netlify and Vercel already do continuous deployment for frontends: push to main and it is live in a minute. The same idea applies to backends, with a few more safety steps.

walk.title: A backend change from merge to production
steps: PR merged to main. CI builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA and pushes it to the registry.
The pipeline deploys that exact image to staging and runs smoke tests (does /healthz work? can a test user log in?).
It promotes the same image (not a rebuild) to production with a rolling or canary deploy.
It watches error rate and latency for 10 minutes.
If errors jump, it rolls back to the previous image automatically and notifies the team.

terms: Always releasable; release is a button.
Every passing change goes live automatically.
The built output that gets deployed (e.g. an image).
Moving the same artifact from one environment to the next.
A quick check that the basics work after deploy.
insights: Deploy when someone can watch the first minutes. Most bad deploys show up in the error rate soon after real traffic reaches them.
Fast rollback is worth more than slow, careful releases.
The fear of deploying is a signal that releases are too big or too manual. Make them smaller, not rarer.

prod.summary: A production CD pipeline builds one immutable artifact (for example a Docker image tagged with the git SHA), promotes that exact artifact through environments, and treats rollback as a normal, tested button. Seniors care about two numbers: how long from merge to production, and how long a rollback takes.
checklist: Images are tagged with the commit SHA (or an immutable digest), never only latest, so you always know what is running.
The same image goes to staging and production; only config changes. Check that no build-time env values (like NEXT_PUBLIC_*) differ per environment, or the build is not really reusable.
Database migrations run as their own step before the new code, and are backward compatible with the old code still running.
After deploy, smoke tests hit real endpoints (/healthz, a login, one read) and fail the pipeline on a non-200.
Rollback is one command (redeploy the previous SHA) and has been practised, not just documented.
Production deploys use a protected environment: limited secrets, optional required reviewers, and an audit trail of who deployed what.
Every deploy is announced (chat or dashboard annotation) so error spikes can be matched to a version.
numbers: GitHub Actions: a job waiting for environment approval fails automatically if not approved within 30 days.
Kubernetes Deployment keeps revisionHistoryLimit: 10 old ReplicaSets by default, which is what kubectl rollout undo uses.
Kubernetes marks a rollout as failed after progressDeadlineSeconds: 600 (10 minutes) without progress, by default.
failures: Staging was fine, production shows the staging API URL in the browser.

The frontend was built once with NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL for staging; Next.js inlines these values at build time, so promotion carried them along. Fix: build per environment for public values, or serve runtime config from the server.
Rollback did not help: the old version crashes with column "status" does not exist.
The new release ran a migration that removed or renamed a column the old code needs. Fix: expand/contract migrations — add first, deploy code, remove old columns only in a later release.
Nobody can tell which commit is in production; the deployment says image: api:latest.
Mutable tags. A node can also pull a different latest on restart. Fix: tag with the SHA or pin the digest, and show the version in /healthz.
Error rate doubles 20 minutes after a Friday deploy and the on-call engineer needs 40 minutes to roll back.
Rollback was manual and never practised. Fix: automatic rollback on health-check or error-rate regression, and a one-click redeploy of the previous SHA.

code.title: GitHub Actions: build once, deploy the same image, smoke test
code.src:
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    permissions: { contents: read, packages: write }
    outputs:
      image: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with: { persist-credentials: false }
      - id: meta  # registry names must be lowercase; the repo name may not be
        run: echo "image=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}:${GITHUB_SHA}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - run: echo "$TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u "$GITHUB_ACTOR" --password-stdin
        env: { TOKEN: "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" }
      - run: docker build -t "$IMAGE" . && docker push "$IMAGE"
        env: { IMAGE: "${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}" }

  deploy-production:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    environment: production   # protection rules + production-only secrets
    concurrency: { group: deploy-production, cancel-in-progress: false }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7   # only for the deploy script, no build here
        with: { persist-credentials: false }
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh "$IMAGE"
        env: { IMAGE: "${{ needs.build.outputs.image }}" }
      - name: Smoke test
        run: curl --fail --retry 5 --retry-delay 5 https://api.example.com/healthz
code.note: The production job never builds; it receives the image name from build. cancel-in-progress: false queues deploys instead of killing one halfway. Values go into run through env, not pasted into the script, which avoids script injection. The deploy job needs its own checkout: jobs run on fresh machines.

qs.s: Your pipeline builds the Docker image again in the production job “to be safe”. The base image is node:22. What is the real risk?
o: Production builds are slower, nothing else
Registries reject two images with the same code
Docker caches make the second build identical anyway
node:22 may point to a newer image than the one you tested, so production runs something never tested
qs.e: Tags like node:22 move. A rebuild can pull a new base image or new transitive packages. Caches on a fresh runner are not guaranteed, so “identical” is an assumption, not a fact.

qs.s: A release adds a NOT NULL column and code that writes it. The deploy fails health checks and rolls back automatically. Users now get 500 errors on signup. Most likely reason?
o: The migration already ran; the old code inserts rows without the new NOT NULL column
The rollback deleted the database
The load balancer cached the new version
Health checks are too strict
qs.e: Rollback restores code, not schema. Add the column as nullable or with a default first, so both versions can write. Make it NOT NULL in a later release.

qs.s: Leadership asks to stop deploying on Fridays after one bad Friday incident. Your team deploys 10 small changes a day with automated rollback. What is the strongest argument?
o: Friday deploys are required by DORA
Weekend traffic is always lower, so incidents do not matter
Holding changes until Monday makes Monday's deploy bigger and riskier; fix the rollback and detection that failed instead
Developers prefer to deploy on Fridays
qs.e: A freeze batches changes, which is the thing CD tries to avoid. The incident showed a gap in detection or rollback; that is what should be fixed. A freeze can still be reasonable for teams without that automation.

qs.s: Read this production deploy job. Two PRs merge 40 seconds apart. The deploy script runs a database migration, then rolls out pods (about 4 minutes). What can go wrong?

code.title: .github/workflows/deploy.yml (excerpt)
code.src:
deploy-production:
  needs: build
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  environment: production
  concurrency:
    group: deploy-production
    cancel-in-progress: true
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v7
    - run: ./scripts/migrate.sh
    - run: ./scripts/rollout.sh "$IMAGE"
      env: { IMAGE: "${{ needs.build.outputs.image }}" }

o: Nothing: the second run waits for the first one
Both deploys run in parallel and the last one wins
GitHub rejects the second workflow run
The first deploy is cancelled halfway, possibly after its migration and in the middle of its rollout, leaving production in a mixed state
qs.e: cancel-in-progress: true kills the running job when a new one joins the group. That is right for PR checks and dangerous for deploys. Use cancel-in-progress: false so deploys queue. (The group still prevents parallel runs, so “both deploys run in parallel” is wrong.)

qs.s: All pods come from the same Deployment, but they report different image digests. Why?

code.title: kubectl output
code.src:
$ kubectl get deploy api -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image} {.spec.template.spec.containers[0].imagePullPolicy}'
ghcr.io/acme/api:latest IfNotPresent

$ kubectl get pods -l app=api -o custom-columns=POD:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,DIGEST:.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID
POD           NODE    DIGEST
api-7c9-abcd  node-a  ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:1f2e9c...
api-7c9-efgh  node-b  ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:9a8b41...
api-7c9-ijkl  node-c  ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:9a8b41...

o: latest is a moving tag and IfNotPresent reuses whatever each node cached earlier, so node-a runs an older build
Kubernetes builds the image separately on each node
The registry returns a random layer order
The pods are in different namespaces
qs.e: With a mutable tag, “the same image” is not guaranteed. A node that already had an older latest keeps using it. Deploy by commit SHA tag or by digest; then every node runs exactly the tested image and rollback means “deploy the previous SHA”.

qs.s: Two teams report their numbers for one month. Team A: 2 deploys, 1 caused an incident. Team B: 200 deploys, 10 caused incidents. Which statement is correct about change failure rate (failed deploys ÷ all deploys)?
o: Team A is safer because it had fewer incidents
Both teams have the same rate
Team B: 5%, Team A: 50%. Team B ships more often and each change is less likely to fail
Change failure rate cannot be compared across teams
qs.e: 10 ÷ 200 = 5%, 1 ÷ 2 = 50%. Counting incidents alone ignores how much change was shipped. This is the DORA pattern: small, frequent deploys tend to fail less often per deploy and are faster to recover.

qs.s: A payments company must prove that every production change was approved by a second person. The team wants to keep automated deploys. Which setup meets the audit and keeps CD?
o: Developers email a change form to the ops team, who deploy manually
A required PR review on protected main, plus a protected production environment with required reviewers; the pipeline log records who approved and what SHA shipped
Deploy only once a month after a change-board meeting
Give only the lead production access and let them deploy from their laptop
qs.e: Approval gates can be automated and leave a better audit trail than manual steps: who reviewed, who approved the deploy, which commit. Manual hand-offs and monthly batches make each change bigger and the record weaker. A laptop deploy has no reliable record at all.

interview.q: Walk me through a CD pipeline you would build for a containerised backend, from merge to production.
answer: On merge: build one image, tag it with the commit SHA, push it, and record its digest. Optionally sign it and generate an SBOM.
Deploy that exact image to staging, run migrations (backward compatible), run smoke tests against real endpoints.
Promote the same digest to production through a protected environment, with a rolling or canary rollout and readiness probes.
Watch error rate and latency against the previous version for a fixed window; roll back automatically on regression.
Annotate dashboards with the deploy, and make rollback a single, practised command: deploy the previous SHA.
Trade-off: more gates mean more safety but slower lead time; automate the gates instead of adding manual steps.
followups: Where do database migrations run, and what if one fails halfway?
How would you handle frontend config that is baked in at build time?

interview.q: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment, and when would you choose delivery?
answer: Delivery: every change on main is deployable, and a person presses the button. Deployment: it goes to production automatically.
Choose delivery when releases must match outside events (app store review, customer contracts, regulated sign-off) or when monitoring is not good enough to trust automatic rollout yet.
Choose deployment when tests, observability and automatic rollback are strong; it gives the smallest batches.
Both need the same base: build once, automated tests, fast rollback. The difference is only the final trigger.
Feature flags reduce the need for a manual button: code can deploy automatically while release stays a business decision.
followups: Which metrics tell you the team is ready to remove the manual button?
How do flags change the answer?

interview.q: A deploy went out, error rate tripled, and rollback did not fix it. What could cause that, and how do you design to avoid it?
answer: Rollback restores code, not data or schema. A migration that dropped or renamed a column, or new-format data, breaks the old version too.
Other one-way changes: messages written to a queue in a new format, cache entries in a new shape, external API contracts changed.
Design: expand/contract migrations (add first, switch code, remove later), readers that accept old and new formats, versioned messages.
Check what else changed at the same time: config, a dependency, infrastructure, a third-party outage. Not every incident is the deploy.
Practise rollback in staging, including the schema state, so it is a tested path.
followups: How would you roll out a column rename with zero downtime?
When would you roll forward instead of back?

one: Ways of replacing the running version with a new one: rolling, blue-green, canary, and their trade-offs.
an: Replacing a restaurant's menu. Rolling: swap one table's menus at a time. Blue-green: open an identical second restaurant and redirect the queue. Canary: give the new menu to a few tables and watch their faces.
how: Rolling: replace instances gradually. Default in Kubernetes. Old and new versions run side by side for a while.
Blue-green: deploy the new version (green) alongside the old (blue), test it, switch all traffic at once. Rollback = switch back. Costs double capacity during the switch.
Canary: send 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% of traffic to the new version, watching error rates and latency at each step; stop automatically if they degrade.
All of them need backward-compatible database changes, because both versions touch the same DB.
why: Zero-downtime deploys and small blast radius are expected at senior level. Choosing a strategy is a trade between safety, cost and complexity.
trade: Canary needs good metrics to judge health, or it is just a slow rollout. Blue-green does not protect against a bad DB migration.

myth.r: It undoes code. Data written by the new version and migrations already applied stay. Plan migrations to be compatible both ways.

q.s: A new version has a bug that only affects 2% of requests. Which strategy most likely catches it before all users see it?
o: Recreate (stop all, start all)
A canary with automated error-rate comparison
Blue-green with a manual switch
Deploying at night
q.e: Canaries expose a small slice of real traffic and compare it to the baseline.

more: Database compatibility across two app versions
lab: On kind, set maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 and roll out a new image while curling the service in a loop: no errors.
Repeat with a readiness probe removed and a slow-starting app; count the errors.
Install Argo Rollouts and run a canary with 20% → 50% → 100% steps.

plain: A deployment strategy is how you replace the old version with the new one while users are using the app. Rolling: replace instances one at a time. Blue-green: start a full copy of the new version, then switch all traffic at once. Canary: send a small percentage of users to the new version first and watch.
bridge: Vercel's preview deployments and instant rollbacks are a form of blue-green: the new version is fully ready before the domain points to it.

walk.title: A canary release catches a bug
steps: Version 2.3 is deployed next to 2.2. The router sends 5% of traffic to 2.3.
Monitoring compares them: 2.2 has 0.2% errors; 2.3 has 3% errors on the /checkout route.
The automated analysis stops the rollout and sends 100% back to 2.2.
Only 5% of users for a few minutes saw the bug, instead of everyone.
The team finds the bug (a missing database column in one region), fixes it, and starts a new canary.

terms: Two full environments; switch traffic between them.
Release to a small slice first and compare.
insights: Get a good rolling update first: readiness probe, graceful shutdown, preStop. Most 502s during deploys come from shutdown, not from the choice of strategy.
Choose by blast radius and cost. Rolling is cheap. Blue-green buys an instant switch back for double capacity. Canary buys early detection, but only if your metrics are good.
Write the abort rule before the rollout starts (for example “5xx rate above stable for 5 minutes”), so nobody argues about it during an incident.

prod.summary: Most teams use a rolling update with readiness probes and graceful shutdown, and add canary analysis for high-risk services. In production the hard parts are not the traffic switch: they are draining old connections without errors, keeping the database compatible with two versions, and having a metric that can actually say “the new version is worse”.
checklist: Readiness probe answers “can this pod serve now?” (started, warmed up, not shutting down). Be careful with shared dependencies: if every pod checks the same database, one database blip removes all pods at once.
Liveness probe checks only the process itself (for example the event loop answers). Never put the database in it, or a database failover restarts every pod.
Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM the app stops accepting new requests, finishes in-flight ones, then exits within terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
A short preStop sleep (a few seconds) so the load balancer removes the pod before it stops listening.
For zero-capacity-loss rollouts, maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1 (or a %); check the cluster has room for the extra pods.
Canary steps have explicit pass/fail metrics (for example 5xx rate and p99 latency compared to the stable version), a minimum request count, and an automatic abort.
Schema changes follow expand/contract so old and new versions can run together during the rollout.
Long-lived connections (WebSockets, SSE) have a reconnect strategy, because every deploy cuts them.
numbers: Kubernetes Deployment defaults: strategy RollingUpdate, maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 25%.
Kubernetes default terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30 seconds before SIGKILL.
Kubernetes default progressDeadlineSeconds is 600; after that the rollout reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded.
failures: A burst of 502/503 errors during every rolling deploy, then it recovers.

Pods stop listening before the load balancer stops sending traffic, or the app exits on SIGTERM without draining. Fix: add a preStop sleep, handle SIGTERM by closing the server gracefully, and use a real readiness probe.
kubectl rollout status prints error: deployment "api" exceeded its progress deadline.
New pods never become Ready: crash loop, failing readiness probe, missing config, or no node capacity for the surge. Check kubectl describe pod events, then kubectl rollout undo.
Canary looked healthy at 5% for 10 minutes, then 100% caused an outage.

The metric was too coarse (overall error rate) or the 5% slice had too few requests for the broken path. Fix: compare per route, require a minimum request count per step, and include latency, not just errors.
After a blue-green switch, users are logged out.
Sessions were stored in memory on the blue instances. Fix: keep session state in a shared store (Redis, DB) or in signed cookies, so either colour can serve any user.

code.title: Kubernetes rolling update without dropped requests
code.src:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  minReadySeconds: 10
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: api }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: api }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/api:3f9c2e1
          ports: [{ containerPort: 3000 }]
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 3000 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              sleep: { seconds: 5 }
code.note: maxUnavailable: 0 keeps full capacity; preStop gives the load balancer time to stop routing before shutdown. The native sleep action is enabled by default since Kubernetes 1.30 (beta) and GA in 1.34; on older clusters use an exec sleep.

qs.s: A Deployment has 8 replicas and the default rolling update settings. During a rollout, at most how many pods can exist, and at least how many must be available?
o: 10 pods total, at least 6 available
8 total, at least 8 available
16 total, at least 4 available
9 total, at least 7 available
qs.e: Defaults are 25%: maxSurge 25% of 8 = 2 (rounded up), so 10 total; maxUnavailable 25% of 8 = 2 (rounded down), so at least 6 available.

qs.s: You must ship a new search engine where wrong results are costly but errors are rare. You want to compare results on real traffic without users seeing the new version. Which approach?
o: Blue-green with an instant switch
Shadow traffic: copy live requests to the new version and compare, but return only the old version's responses
Rolling update with maxSurge: 100%
Canary at 50%
qs.e: Canaries show the new version to real users. Shadowing (dark launch) exercises it with real traffic while users only see the old result. Be careful with side effects: shadowed writes must be disabled.

qs.s: A team uses blue-green. The new version includes a migration that drops a column. They switch to green, see bugs, and switch back to blue within 2 minutes. What happens?
o: Everything is fine; blue-green rollback is instant
Blue works but serves stale cache
Green keeps running in the background
Blue fails on queries that use the dropped column, because both colours share the database
qs.e: Blue-green duplicates app servers, not the database. Destructive schema changes must happen in a later release, after no running version needs the column.

qs.s: Every rolling deploy produces a burst of 502 errors. Read the shutdown code. What is wrong?

code.title: server.ts

o: Nothing: exit code 0 tells Kubernetes the shutdown was clean
It exits immediately, cutting in-flight requests; it should stop accepting connections with server.close(), wait for running requests, then exit (with a timeout below the grace period)
Kubernetes sends SIGKILL, not SIGTERM, so this handler never runs
process.exit(0) makes Kubernetes restart the pod in a loop
qs.e: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM first and waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 s default) before SIGKILL. Exiting at once drops requests that are still running. Combine server.close() with a preStop sleep, because the load balancer may still send new requests for a few seconds after SIGTERM.

qs.s: Postgres has a 60-second failover. Read the probe. What happens to the API during the failover?

code.title: deployment.yaml (excerpt)
code.src:
containers:
  - name: api
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 3000 }  # /healthz runs SELECT 1 on Postgres
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 3000 }
      periodSeconds: 5

o: Nothing: probes ignore database errors
Only new pods are affected
After about 30 seconds the kubelet restarts every API pod; they come back cold and all reconnect at once, making recovery slower
Kubernetes fails over the database too
qs.e: 3 failures × 10 s = 30 s, then the container is killed and restarted, on every pod, because they all share the database. Restarting cannot fix a database problem. Liveness should test only the process; let requests fail fast (or return 503) while the database recovers.

qs.s: Your API serves 1,000 requests per minute. A canary gets 2% of traffic for 10 minutes. A bug affects only one route, which is 1% of all requests. How many requests to that route does the canary see?
o: About 2
About 20
About 200
About 0.2
qs.e: 1,000 × 2% = 20 canary requests per minute, × 10 minutes = 200 canary requests, × 1% = 2 on the broken route. Two requests cannot prove anything. Require a minimum sample per step, compare per route, or hold the canary longer or at a higher percentage.

qs.s: You change a background worker that consumes jobs from a queue (no HTTP traffic). There are 10 worker pods. How do you canary it?
o: You cannot; canaries only work for HTTP traffic
Blue-green: switch all consumers at once
Use a feature flag on the HTTP router
Run 1 new-version worker next to 9 old ones (about 10% of jobs), compare its job error rate and duration, then scale up; make sure both versions understand the job format
qs.e: Competing consumers split the jobs, so the replica ratio is the traffic split. The extra rule for queues: messages written by one version must be readable by the other, in both directions, because rollback leaves new-format jobs in the queue.

interview.q: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments. When would you pick each?
answer: Rolling: default in Kubernetes, no extra environment, gradual. Both versions serve at once; rollback is another rollout, not instant.
Blue-green: full second copy, instant switch and instant switch-back. Costs double capacity for a while and does not protect the shared database.
Canary: small slice of real traffic, compared with the stable version on metrics, automatic abort. Needs good per-version metrics and enough traffic.
All three need backward-compatible schema and message formats, and graceful shutdown.
Pick by risk and traffic: rolling for most services, canary for high-traffic critical paths, blue-green when you need instant cut-over (for example a big infrastructure change).
followups: How does a canary decide “worse”, statistically?
Where do feature flags fit compared to canaries?

interview.q: How do you get truly zero-downtime deploys on Kubernetes? Users see 502s today.
answer: Readiness probe so traffic only reaches pods that can serve; liveness probe that does not depend on shared services.
Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close DB pools, exit before the grace period ends.
preStop sleep of a few seconds, because endpoint removal and the load balancer update happen in parallel with SIGTERM.
maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1, and a PodDisruptionBudget for node drains.
Keep-alive and long connections: make clients retry idempotent requests; WebSocket clients must reconnect.
followups: Why can the pod still receive requests after it got SIGTERM?
How do you test this before production?

interview.q: Design the rollout of a schema change, renaming a column, with zero downtime and safe rollback.
answer: Expand: add the new column (nullable), deploy code that writes both columns and reads the old one.
Backfill in batches (avoid long locks), then deploy code that reads the new column, still writing both.
Wait until no running or rollback-target version needs the old column.
Contract: stop writing the old column, then drop it in a later release.
At every step, the previous version still works, so rollback is safe. Trade-off: several deploys and temporary double writes.
followups: How do you backfill 500 million rows without hurting production?
What about a NOT NULL constraint on the new column?

sequenceDiagram

  participant D as Deployment
  participant N as New pod
  participant L as Load balancer
  participant O as Old pod
  loop For each of 4 replicas
    D->>N: Start 1 extra pod (maxSurge 1)

diagrams.caption: What to notice: with maxUnavailable: 0 a new pod must be Ready before an old one stops. The preStop sleep gives the load balancer time to stop sending traffic before the app receives SIGTERM.

codeCheck.detail: Deployment passes kubeconform -strict for 1.34 (fails on 1.28, where preStop sleep does not exist, as the note says). Practice: ran server.ts with 3 slow in-flight requests and SIGTERM; all 3 failed with a socket error, and all 3 got 200 with server.close().

one: Runtime switches that turn code paths on or off, per user or percentage, without a deploy.
an: Light switches installed during construction. The wiring is done (deployed), but you decide when to flip the lights on (release).
how: if (flags.newCheckout(user)) { ... }. The flag service decides per user: internal staff, 5% of users, users in Korea.
Separates deploy (code is in production) from release (users see it). Enables trunk-based development, gradual rollouts, A/B tests and instant kill switches.
Tools: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, GrowthBook, Flagsmith, or a simple DB table.
why: Turning off a broken feature in seconds beats a 15-minute rollback. Product can launch on a schedule independent of engineering deploys.
trade: Flags are debt: every flag doubles the code paths to test. Remove them once fully rolled out; give each one an owner and an expiry.

myth.r: Their most valuable uses are safe rollout and the kill switch.

q.s: A codebase has 300 flags, most at 100% for over a year. Problem?
o: None
Dead branches and combinatorial complexity; old flags should be removed
They slow down DNS
They break CORS
q.e: Each stale flag is untested dead code and a trap. Make cleanup part of the rollout definition of done.

more: Flag types: release, experiment, ops (kill switch), permission
lab: Implement a tiny flag system: a table flags(name, enabled, rollout_percent) and isEnabled(name, userId) using a hash of the user ID for stable bucketing.
Roll a fake feature to 10%, then 50%; check the same user stays in the same bucket.
Try GrowthBook or Unleash locally and compare.

plain:
A feature flag is an if in your code whose value you can change while the app is running, without a deploy. You can turn a feature on for your team, for 10% of users, for one country, or off for everyone in seconds.

This separates deploying code (it is on the server) from releasing a feature (users see it).
bridge: You probably have something like this already: if (user.isBetaTester). Flag systems make that idea general, remote-controlled and safe.

walk.title: Using a flag as an emergency switch
steps: A new recommendations widget is released to 100% behind the flag recs-v2.
On Friday evening, the recommendations service starts timing out and slowing the homepage.
On-call engineer opens the flag dashboard and turns recs-v2 off.
Within seconds, the homepage stops calling the service and is fast again. No deploy, no rollback.
On Monday the team fixes the service and turns the flag back on gradually.

terms: A runtime switch for a code path.
The share of users who see the feature.
A flag used to turn something off quickly in emergencies.
Old flags that should have been removed.
insights: Changing a flag in production is a deploy without CI. It deserves the same care: an audit log, a reason, and a way back.
Know which kind of flag you are adding. A release flag should be gone in weeks; a kill switch may stay for years on purpose.
The kill switch alone justifies flags for risky features.

prod.summary: In production, flags are evaluated server-side from a local cache with a safe default, bucketed by a stable user ID, and treated as code that expires. Seniors care about: what happens when the flag service is down, whether a user sees the same variant everywhere, and how many stale flags exist.
checklist: Every flag has a type (release, experiment, ops kill switch, permission), an owner and a removal date.
Code passes a safe default value that is used when the flag service cannot be reached.
Evaluation is local (SDK caches rules and streams updates); no network call per request.
Percentage rollouts hash a stable ID (user or account) together with the flag key, so the same user stays in the same bucket.
Client-side flags expose only the value, not targeting rules that may leak unreleased features or customer lists.
Flag changes in production are audited and, for risky flags, need approval like a deploy.
Removing a flag at 100% is part of the feature's definition of done.
numbers: OpenFeature, the vendor-neutral flag API, has been a CNCF incubating project since November 2023.
With a 1% rollout on 50,000 daily users, about 500 users see the feature — often too few to judge a rare error on one route.
failures: Users report the new checkout appearing and disappearing on refresh.
Bucketing used Math.random() or a session ID instead of a stable user ID. Fix: hash flagKey + userId and use the same ID on server and client.
The flag service had an outage and a disabled, half-finished feature became visible to everyone.
The code default was true or the SDK fell back to “on”. Fix: defaults are always the safe, old behaviour; test the “service unreachable” path.
p99 latency rose by 80 ms after adding flags.
Each request called the flag API over the network. Fix: use an SDK that evaluates locally from a cached rule set and streams updates.
Someone removes an old flag and an unrelated feature breaks.
Two flags were nested and the other code path had never been tested. Fix: keep flags independent, remove them soon after 100%, and search for every usage before removal.

code.title: Stable percentage bucketing
code.note: Including the flag key in the hash means a user in the first 10% of one flag is not automatically in the first 10% of every flag.

qs.s: You roll out new-search from 10% to 30%. A user who already had the feature at 10% complains it disappeared. Bucketing is hash(userId) % 100 < percent. What is most likely wrong?
o: Percent rollouts always reshuffle users
The hash function is too slow
The flag service is down
Something other than userId was hashed in one place (for example an anonymous or session ID), so the user's bucket is not stable
qs.e: With a stable hash, raising the percent only adds users; nobody below the old threshold is removed. Losing it means the input ID changed, often logged-out vs logged-in or server vs client using different IDs.

qs.s: The recommendations widget is slowing the homepage at 2 a.m. It shipped 3 weeks ago behind recs-v2, now at 100%. What is the fastest safe action?
o: Roll back to the deploy from 3 weeks ago
Scale the recommendations service up
Turn off recs-v2 (the kill switch), then investigate
Hotfix the widget and deploy
qs.e: A code rollback 3 weeks back would undo many unrelated changes. The flag removes the risky path in seconds. Scaling may help, but it is a guess under pressure.

qs.s: A team evaluates all flags in the browser with the full rule set downloaded from the vendor. A security review complains. Why?
o: The rules can reveal unreleased feature names and targeting data (like customer IDs or emails) to anyone with DevTools
Browsers cannot compute hashes
Client-side flags are always slower
It breaks server-side rendering
qs.e: Anything sent to the browser is public. Evaluate on the server, or use a client SDK mode that sends only the evaluated values for this user.

qs.s: The flag service is unreachable for 20 minutes. new-pricing is configured for 5% of users. What do users see during the outage?

code.title: pricing.ts (OpenFeature SDK)

o: 5% see the new pricing, as configured
Nobody sees it, because the flag cannot be evaluated
Everyone sees the new pricing, because the code default is true and the SDK returns it when evaluation fails
The request throws and checkout fails
qs.e: The second argument is the default returned when the flag cannot be evaluated (provider down, flag missing). Here an outage turns a 5% rollout into 100%. Defaults must be the safe, old behaviour: false. (SDKs with a local cache may keep the last known rules for a while, but you cannot rely on that for a cold start.)

qs.s: Two experiments run at the same time: new-search at 10% and new-checkout at 10%. Checkout conversion in the test group is up 8%. Read the bucketing code. Why can you not trust that result?

code.title: flags.ts

o: murmur32 is not random enough
The hash ignores the flag key, so the same 10% of users get both features; the uplift may come from the new search
10% is always too small for an experiment
Percentages above 5% are not allowed for experiments
qs.e: Without the flag key (or a salt) in the hash, every flag picks the same users. The two experiments are fully overlapped, so their effects are mixed. Hash flagKey:userId so assignment is independent per flag.

qs.s: A Next.js page evaluates the new-hero flag in the browser after hydration. Users complain that the old banner shows for a moment, then jumps to the new one. Best fix?
o: Add a CSS transition so the change looks smooth
Cache the flag in localStorage
Evaluate a second time after 1 second
Evaluate the flag on the server for this request and render the right variant in the HTML (or bootstrap the client SDK with the server's values)
qs.e: Client-only evaluation means the first paint uses the default, then re-renders: flicker and layout shift, and it hurts experiment data too. Server evaluation gives one consistent answer. localStorage still shows the wrong variant on first visit or after a change.

qs.s: recs-v2 has been at 100% for 2 months. To clean up, an engineer archives the flag in the dashboard on Monday and plans to remove the code on Friday. What happens on Monday?
o: The SDK returns the code default (false) for a missing flag, so the feature disappears for everyone until Friday
Nothing: archived flags keep their last value
The app crashes because the flag is missing
Only new users lose the feature
qs.e: Order matters: first remove the flag check from the code (keeping the new path), deploy, confirm no evaluations, then archive the flag. Most SDKs treat an unknown flag as “use the default”, which for a release flag is the old behaviour.

interview.q: How would you design a feature-flag system for a company with 50 services?
answer: Use a vendor or OpenFeature-compatible open-source tool rather than building the core; standardise on one SDK interface (OpenFeature) to avoid lock-in.
Local evaluation: SDKs cache rules and stream updates, so a flag check is in-memory and the flag service can be down without taking services down.
Safe defaults in code, stable bucketing by user or account ID plus flag key, the same ID on server and client.
Governance: flag types, owners, expiry dates, audit log, approvals for production changes on risky flags.
Clean-up: alerts for flags at 100% or 0% for weeks, and removal in the definition of done.
followups: How do you keep flag evaluation consistent between frontend and backend?
How do you test code with many flags?

interview.q: Feature flags vs canary deployments: which do you use for what?
answer: Canary controls which version of the binary serves traffic; it catches crashes, latency, memory leaks from the whole deploy.
Flags control which code path a user gets, inside one version; they target by user, tenant or region and switch in seconds.
Canary is about deploy risk; flags are about release risk and business control (beta customers, experiments, kill switches).
They combine well: canary every deploy, and put risky features behind a flag that rolls out separately.
Flags cost code complexity and need cleanup; canaries need infrastructure and metrics.
followups: Can a flag protect you from a bad database migration?
How would you run an A/B test with flags correctly?

interview.q: Your codebase has 400 flags and engineers are afraid to touch them. How do you fix it?
answer: Inventory: for each flag, last change date, current value, evaluation count, owner. Many will be at 100% or 0% for months.
Remove stale release flags first: code change keeping the live path, deploy, then archive the flag. Never the other order.
Separate long-lived flags (ops kill switches, permissions) from temporary ones, and document them as config.
Prevent recurrence: expiry dates with reminders or failing lint checks, flag removal in the definition of done.
Avoid nested and dependent flags; test the default path, because that is what runs when the service is down.
followups: Should permission or entitlement checks live in a flag system?
How do you find all usages of a flag safely?

diagrams.caption: What to notice: no network call per request, and every failure path ends in the old behaviour. The bucket depends only on the flag key and user ID, so the same user always gets the same answer.

sequenceDiagram

  participant F as Flag service
  participant A as App (SDK)
  participant R as Recs service

Practice: the OpenFeature snippet with a failing provider gave new pricing to 1000/1000 users; the murmur3 snippet put 100% of one test group in the other.
