one: Running the same code in dev, staging and production, with differences expressed only through configuration.
an: The same play performed in rehearsal and on opening night. The script never changes; only the venue and audience do.
how: The Twelve-Factor App rules most teams follow: config in environment variables, not code; stateless processes; backing services (DB, cache) attached via URLs; logs to stdout; dev/prod parity.
Staging should mirror production closely (same infra types, realistic data volume) or it catches little.
Preview environments: every PR gets its own temporary deployment (Vercel, Netlify, Render).
why: "It worked in staging" bugs come from differences between environments. Config-driven deploys remove a class of mistakes.
trade: Full production parity is expensive. Be explicit about where staging differs.

myth.r: Environment-name checks hide behaviour. Prefer explicit config values (FEATURE_X_ENABLED, PAYMENT_API_URL).

o: Reading DATABASE_URL from env
Hard-coding the production DB host in source code
Logging to stdout
Stateless processes
q.e: Config belongs in the environment, so the same build runs anywhere.

more: Config validation at startup (fail fast on missing env vars)
Production-like staging data without real personal data
Config vs secrets vs feature flags
Environment parity for background workers too
lab: Read all twelve factors and score one of your own apps against each.
Add startup validation with Zod: parse process.env into a typed config object and exit with a clear message if something is missing.

plain:
Your app runs in several environments: development (your laptop), staging (a test copy of production) and production (real users). The code should be identical in all of them; only the configuration changes: database URL, API keys, feature settings.

Configuration comes from environment variables, not from values written in the code.
bridge: .env.local in your frontend and the environment variable settings in Netlify are this idea. Different values per environment, same code.

walk.title: Catching a missing setting before it hurts
steps: Production needs PAYMENT_API_KEY, but someone forgot to set it for the new region.
Bad version: the app starts fine, and crashes only when the first customer tries to pay.
Good version: at startup, the app validates all config with a schema (e.g. Zod).
It immediately exits with “Missing required env var PAYMENT_API_KEY”.
The deploy fails its health check and is rolled back automatically. No customer ever saw the problem.

terms: A named value given to a program from outside, like DATABASE_URL.
A production-like environment for final testing.
A well-known set of rules for building deployable apps.
A temporary deployment for one pull request.
insights: For every config value ask: build time or run time? Build-time values are frozen into the artifact and break “build once, deploy everywhere”.
When a bug appears only in production, first compare config and versions between environments. The difference is usually the cause.
NODE_ENV tells libraries how to behave (optimised or debug). It is not the name of your environment; use a separate variable like APP_ENV.

prod.summary: In production, config is typed, validated at startup, and different per environment only where it must be. Seniors check three things: the app refuses to start with bad config, staging is close enough to production to catch real bugs, and build-time config is not silently baked into an artifact that is meant to be reused.
checklist: Startup parses all env vars into a typed config object (for example with Zod) and exits with a clear message if anything is missing or invalid.
Code reads config only through that object, never process.env.X scattered across files. Required values have no silent fallback.
Each environment has its own database, credentials and third-party accounts (payment sandbox in staging, never live keys).
Every deployed environment (staging too) runs with NODE_ENV=production; the environment name lives in a separate variable such as APP_ENV.
Build-time variables (NEXT_PUBLIC_*, VITE_*) are listed; anyone promoting one artifact through environments knows they are frozen at build time.
Preview environments for PRs use seeded or anonymised data and their own database (or database branch), never a copy of production personal data.
Differences between staging and production (smaller DB, no CDN, fewer replicas) are written down.
.env* files with real values are in .gitignore; a committed .env.example lists every variable.
numbers: Next.js inlines NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables into the JS bundle at next build; after the build the app no longer responds to changes in them.
Next.js env lookup order: process.env, then .env.$(NODE_ENV).local, .env.local (not in test), .env.$(NODE_ENV), .env. A variable already set in the shell wins over every file.
Next.js expects NODE_ENV to be production, development or test and prints a warning for any other value.
failures: Production crashes on the first payment with TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined, hours after a successful deploy.
A required env var was missing and nothing checked it at startup. Fix: validate config on boot and exit non-zero, so the health check fails and the deploy is rolled back.
PORT is set to "8080" but the app compares port === 8080 and binds to the default.
Env vars are always strings. Fix: coerce types in the config schema (z.coerce.number()), and use explicit boolean parsing; Boolean("false") is true.
A staging test sent real emails to real customers.
Staging used a copy of production data and a live email provider key. Fix: anonymise data and use a sandbox or catch-all mail service outside production.
A bug only happens in production: staging never shows it.
Parity gap, for example SQLite or a single instance in staging, Postgres and 6 replicas in production. Fix: same backing services and versions, at least 2 replicas in staging so stateful bugs appear.

code.title: Typed config, validated at startup (Zod)
code.note: The enum + transform avoids the classic bug where the string "false" is truthy. min(1) matters too: an empty PORT= is coerced to 0, and listen(0) picks a random port, so the app “starts” but no probe ever reaches it.

qs.s: One Docker image of a Next.js app is promoted from staging to production. In production, the browser still calls the staging analytics ID from NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID, although the production env var is correct. Why?
o: The CDN cached the old env var
Production env vars need a restart
NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are inlined into the JS bundle during next build, so the staging value is inside the image
Next.js ignores env vars in Docker
qs.e: Public values are compiled into the client bundle. For build-once images, expose runtime values through a server API or a server component, or build per environment.

qs.s: A config line reads const debug = Boolean(process.env.DEBUG). Ops sets DEBUG=false in production. What happens?
o: Debug mode is on, because any non-empty string is truthy
Debug mode is off
The app throws on startup
It depends on NODE_ENV
qs.e: Env vars are strings. "false" is a non-empty string, so it is truthy. Parse booleans explicitly against the allowed strings.

qs.s: Your staging database is 2 GB; production is 900 GB. A new query passes all staging tests and is fast there. What risk is the team ignoring?
o: Staging uses a different Postgres version
Query plans and timings change with data size; a sequential scan fine on 2 GB can time out on 900 GB
Staging should not run queries
Production has more CPU, so it will be faster
qs.e: Parity covers data volume too. Test heavy queries against production-sized (anonymised) data or check EXPLAIN plans against production statistics.

qs.s: Production was deployed to a new region without PAYMENT_API_KEY. The app started fine and checkout “works”, but no money arrives. Read the config. Why?

code.title: config.ts

o: The fallbacks silently used the sandbox key and URL, so payments went to the test account; required config must fail at startup instead
The payment provider was down
|| and ?? behave the same, so the key was empty
Env vars are not read in new regions until a restart
qs.e: A default for a required value turns a loud deploy failure into a silent business failure. Defaults are fine for harmless values (like PORT); credentials and URLs of real services must be required and validated, so the pod fails its health check and the rollout stops.

qs.s: A developer runs the Next.js app locally. Which database does it connect to?

code.title: terminal
code.src:
$ cat .env.local
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/dev

$ export DATABASE_URL=postgres://app@prod-db.internal:5432/app   # left over from debugging
$ npm run dev

o: The local dev database, because .env.local has the highest priority
Neither: Next.js refuses to start with two values
The production database, because values already in process.env win over .env files
The local database in development mode, production only after next build
qs.e: Next.js (and dotenv by default) never overrides a variable that is already set in the process environment. A leftover shell export silently points local code at production. Use separate credentials per environment, so a laptop cannot reach production at all.

qs.s: Fifteen PR preview environments all share one staging database. PR A's migration drops a column; four other previews start failing. What is the best fix?
o: Forbid migrations in PRs
Run migrations only on Fridays
Make previews read-only
Give each preview its own database (a seeded schema, a container, or a database branch) that is created and deleted with the preview
qs.e: Shared mutable state couples environments that should be independent. A database per preview isolates schema changes. Forbidding migrations just moves the problem to after merge, and read-only previews cannot test most features.

qs.s: Staging runs with NODE_ENV=development “to get better error pages”. A load test shows staging is 3× slower than production on the same hardware. What is the most likely reason?
o: Staging has less data
NODE_ENV changes library behaviour: development builds of React, no view caching in Express, extra checks; staging is not testing the production code path
The load test tool is broken
Development mode logs to a file
qs.e: Many libraries switch to slower, more verbose code when NODE_ENV is not production. Use NODE_ENV=production in every deployed environment and a separate variable (like APP_ENV=staging or LOG_LEVEL) for real differences.

interview.q: How do you manage configuration for a service that runs in dev, staging, preview and production?
answer: Config from the environment (12-factor), parsed once at startup into a typed object; invalid or missing values stop the process.
Separate secrets (from a secret manager) from plain config; same variable names in every environment, different values.
Build once and inject runtime config; list any build-time values (NEXT_PUBLIC_*) that break this and handle them explicitly.
Name settings by behaviour (EMAIL_PROVIDER=sandbox), not by environment checks scattered in code.
Keep .env.example and validation schema as the documentation; review config changes like code.
followups: How do you handle a config value that must change without a redeploy?
Where does feature-flag config end and app config begin?

interview.q: How close should staging be to production, and how do you decide where it can differ?
answer: Same artifact, same runtime, same backing services and versions (no SQLite for Postgres), same infrastructure code.
It may differ in size (fewer replicas, smaller DB) if that is written down, but keep at least 2 replicas to catch state and concurrency bugs.
Data: anonymised or synthetic; for query performance, test on production-sized data or check plans against production statistics.
Third parties: sandboxes, never live keys; outgoing email to a catch-all.
Decide by asking which bug classes staging must catch, and accept that some only show in production: so also invest in canaries and observability.
followups: Is a shared staging environment still useful when every PR has a preview?
How do you keep staging data fresh and safe?

interview.q: A Next.js app must run as one Docker image in staging and production, but it uses NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL. How do you solve it?
answer: Understand the cause: NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are inlined into the client bundle at build time, so one image carries one value.
Option 1: do not expose it; call the API through same-origin routes (rewrites or route handlers), so the browser never needs the URL.
Option 2: read the value on the server at request time (server components, a /config endpoint) and pass it to the client.
Option 3: build one image per environment and accept that you promote source, not artifacts, for this part; document it.
Trade-off: runtime config adds a request or a server dependency; per-environment builds break “test what you ship”.
followups: What about values used during static generation?
How do you prevent a secret from getting a NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix by mistake?

videos.why: The twelve factors, each with a practical example.

videos.t: What is 12-Factor App? | Twelve Factor App Methodology Explained | KodeKloud
videos.why: Longer walk through the same twelve factors.

one: Keeping API keys, DB passwords and signing keys out of code and logs, delivering them only to the processes that need them, and rotating them.
an: A key safe with a log of who opened it, not a key under the doormat.
how: Never commit secrets. Use the platform's secret store (GitHub Actions secrets, Netlify/Vercel env, AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, Doppler, 1Password).
Frontend has no secrets: anything in a JS bundle (NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_, EXPO_PUBLIC_) is public. Paid API calls must go through your server.
Rotate on schedule and immediately on suspected leak. Scan repos for secrets (GitHub push protection, gitleaks).
Git history keeps secrets forever: removing the line in a new commit does not unleak it. Rotate the key.
why: Leaked keys are found by bots within minutes of a public push. Drained LLM/API credits and cloud bills are a common outcome.
trade: More secure setups (short-lived dynamic credentials) add moving parts. Start with: none in code, none in bundles, least privilege, rotation possible.

myth.m: The key is hidden because it is in an env var.
myth.r: Env vars prefixed for the client get compiled into the bundle and anyone can read them in DevTools.

q.s: A mobile app calls an LLM API directly using a key in an EXPO_PUBLIC_ variable. Correct fix?
o: Obfuscate the key
Move the call behind your own backend, which holds the key and enforces per-user limits; rotate the leaked key
Use a longer key
Base64 encode it
q.e: Anything shipped to the client can be extracted. Rotation is necessary because the old key is already public.

more: Rotation without downtime (two valid keys at once)

plain:
Secrets are values that give access: API keys, database passwords, signing keys. They must never be in your code, never in your git history, and never in anything shipped to a browser or phone.

Store them in your platform's secret settings, give each program only the secrets it needs, and be ready to replace (rotate) any of them quickly.

walk.title: What happens after a key leaks
steps: A developer commits .env with an AI provider key to a public repo.
Within minutes, bots that scan GitHub find it and start using it.
Deleting the file in a new commit does not help: the key is still in git history and already copied.
Correct response: revoke the key at the provider immediately, create a new one, put it in the platform's secret store, redeploy.
Prevention: secret scanning with push protection, .env in .gitignore, and paid API calls only from your server.

terms: A value that grants access and must stay private.
Replacing a secret with a new one and disabling the old.
A service that stores and delivers secrets securely.
GitHub blocking a push that contains a known secret format.
insights: The best secret is one that does not exist: OIDC for CI, cloud roles for workloads, short-lived tokens instead of long-lived keys.
Assume a leaked secret is already being used. Rotate first, investigate second.
Set spending limits and usage alerts on every paid API; they limit the damage of a leak.

prod.summary: In production, secrets live in a managed store, reach only the processes that need them, are never in client bundles or logs, and can be rotated without downtime. Seniors aim to remove long-lived secrets entirely where possible (for example CI deploying to the cloud with OIDC short-lived tokens) and assume any leaked key is already being used.
checklist: No secret in git, Docker image layers or build args, client bundles (NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_, EXPO_PUBLIC_) or logs. Docker builds get secrets with RUN --mount=type=secret.
Secret scanning with push protection is on for every repo; a gitleaks run is part of CI.
Each service and environment has its own credentials with least privilege; staging keys cannot touch production.
Rotation is possible without downtime: the system accepts the old and the new secret during an overlap window.
CI deploys with short-lived OIDC credentials where the cloud supports it, and the cloud trust policy is limited to one repository and branch or environment.
Paid APIs have spending limits and usage alerts, so a leak costs a capped amount.
Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted at rest (or synced from an external manager) and access to them is limited by RBAC.
failures: Provider dashboard shows thousands of API calls per minute from unknown IPs, and the bill is climbing.

The key leaked (public repo, client bundle, or log). Fix order: revoke/rotate the key now, then deploy the new one, then find the leak path. Removing the commit does not help; the key is already copied.
A PR from a fork fails: the deploy-preview step gets an empty API_TOKEN.

numbers: GitHub Actions: a secret is limited to 48 KB; up to 100 repository secrets, 100 environment secrets and 1,000 organization secrets.

qs.s: A developer finds an AWS key in a commit pushed to a public repo 3 hours ago. They want to rewrite git history with git filter-repo first. What is the right first step?
o: Rewrite history, then rotate
Deactivate the key in AWS and check CloudTrail for its use; clean history later
Make the repo private
Add the file to .gitignore
qs.e: Bots scan public pushes within minutes; assume the key is already copied. Revoking stops the damage now. History rewriting and going private do not un-leak a copied key.

qs.s: Your GitHub Actions workflow stores long-lived AWS access keys as secrets to deploy. What change reduces the impact of a leak the most?
o: Rename the secrets
Store the keys base64-encoded
Rotate them once a year
Use GitHub's OIDC token to assume an AWS role with short-lived credentials, restricted to this repo and branch
qs.e: With OIDC there is no stored cloud key to leak, and credentials expire after the job. Base64 is encoding, not encryption; yearly rotation still leaves a long exposure window.

qs.s: In Kubernetes, a teammate says “Secrets are safe, they are encrypted”. You run kubectl get secret db -o yaml and see password: cG9zdGdyZXM=. What is true?
o: It is encrypted with the cluster CA key
It is a hash and cannot be reversed
It is base64; anyone who can read the Secret can decode it, and etcd stores it unencrypted unless encryption at rest is set up
It is only readable by the pod that mounts it
qs.e: cG9zdGdyZXM= decodes to postgres. Protection comes from RBAC, encryption at rest, and ideally an external secret manager.

qs.s: A Dockerfile needs a private npm token. The .npmrc is deleted in the same RUN. Is the token safe in the published image?

code.title: Dockerfile
code.src:
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
ARG NPM_TOKEN
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}" > .npmrc \
 && npm ci \
 && rm .npmrc
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

o: Yes: the file is removed in the same layer, so nothing remains
No: build-arg values used by RUN are visible in the image history (docker history); pass it with RUN --mount=type=secret instead
Yes: ARG values are encrypted by Docker
No, but only because COPY . . copies the local .npmrc
qs.e: Deleting the file in the same layer is good, but Docker's own docs warn that build args are not for secrets: their values can be read from the image metadata. A secret mount exists only during that one RUN and is never stored. (A local .npmrc in the build context is a second risk: keep it in .dockerignore.)

qs.s: Read this step. GitHub masks secrets in logs. Is the log output safe?

code.title: workflow step
code.src:
- name: Get deploy token
  env:
    CLIENT_ID: deploy-bot
    CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.CLIENT_SECRET }}
  run: |
    TOKEN=$(curl -fsS -u "$CLIENT_ID:$CLIENT_SECRET" \
      -d grant_type=client_credentials \
      https://auth.example.com/oauth/token | jq -r .access_token)
    echo "Got access token: $TOKEN"
    echo "DEPLOY_TOKEN=$TOKEN" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

o: No: the access token is a new value that GitHub never registered as a secret, so it is printed in clear; mask it with ::add-mask:: right after you get it, and do not echo it
Yes: GitHub masks every value that was derived from a secret
Yes: the access token expires in an hour, so printing it is harmless
No, but only because curl -u prints the client secret in the log
qs.e: Masking is a string match. The runner registers each secret plus a few encodings of it (base64, JSON- and URL-escaped), so echo $CLIENT_SECRET or a base64 of it shows ***. The access token is a different string, so it appears in full, and anyone who can read the logs (everyone, on a public repo) can use it until it expires. Run echo "::add-mask::$TOKEN" before any output. curl -u does not print the password unless you add -v.

qs.s: You must rotate the Postgres password used by 30 API pods, with zero downtime. Postgres allows one password per role. Which plan works?
o: Change the password, then restart all pods as fast as possible
Keep the old password but make it longer
Change the password at night when traffic is low
Create a second role with the same grants and a new password, roll the pods to the new credentials, check that no sessions use the old role, then disable the old role
qs.e: Changing a single password breaks every pod that has not restarted yet, and existing pools fail on reconnect. Two alternating roles give an overlap window (AWS Secrets Manager's “alternating users” rotation works this way). Check pg_stat_activity before disabling the old role.

code.title: IAM trust policy (Condition)

o: None: OIDC tokens are short-lived
The audience is wrong, so no one can assume the role
Any workflow in any acme repository, on any branch, can assume the production role; restrict sub to one repo and environment, for example repo:acme/api:environment:production
Only forks can assume it
qs.e: Short-lived credentials still need a narrow trust policy. The sub claim says which repo, branch or environment asked for the token; a wildcard on the whole organisation lets any repo (including a test repo or a feature branch) deploy to production.

interview.q: An API key was pushed to a public GitHub repo an hour ago. Walk me through your response.
answer: Revoke or rotate the key at the provider immediately; assume bots already copied it (public pushes are scanned within minutes).
Deploy the new key from the secret store, and check nothing still depends on the old one.
Investigate use: provider logs or audit trail (for AWS, CloudTrail) for calls from unknown IPs, new resources, data access; contain any damage.
Clean git history only after rotation, and know that forks and caches may keep it anyway.
Prevent: push protection and secret scanning, .env in .gitignore, spending limits, and a short blameless review of how it happened.

interview.q: How should CI/CD get access to the cloud to deploy? Compare options.

OIDC federation: the CI job gets a signed token, exchanges it for short-lived cloud credentials; nothing long-lived to store.
Scope the trust: audience, repository, branch or environment in the sub claim; give the role least privilege.
Protect production further with a protected environment (required reviewers, branch restrictions).
Trade-off: OIDC needs per-cloud setup and careful policy review; a wrong wildcard is as bad as a leaked key.

Make apps reload secrets without a full redeploy where possible (file watch from a mounted secret, or a short cache from the secret manager).
Automate it on a schedule so the path is tested before an emergency.

one: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking changes, new features, bug fixes. Plus lockfiles that pin the exact tree you tested.
an: A product's model number that tells you whether the new one still fits your old charger.
how: 2.4.1 → 2.4.2 fix, → 2.5.0 new compatible feature, → 3.0.0 breaking. Ranges: ^2.4.1 means >=2.4.1 <3.0.0; ~2.4.1 means >=2.4.1 <2.5.0.
Below 1.0.0 the caret is stricter: ^0.2.3 allows only 0.2.x, and ^0.0.3 allows only 0.0.3. Semver says anything may change in 0.y.z.
Lockfiles (package-lock, pnpm-lock) record exact resolved versions. CI should install with npm ci, which fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree and never rewrites them.
Automated update PRs (Dependabot, Renovate) keep you current in small steps.
why: Dependency upgrades left for two years become a quarter-long project. Small regular updates are cheap.
trade: Semver is a promise humans sometimes break. Tests and lockfiles are the actual safety net.

myth.m: A minor update cannot break anything.
myth.r: It is not supposed to. Lockfiles and CI exist because it sometimes does.

q.s: Tests pass on your laptop but fail in CI because CI installed a different version of a library. What is the most likely cause?
o: The lockfile is not committed or not used, so CI resolves the newest version in the semver range
CI machines have a different CPU
The CI cache is too large
The library uses tilde ranges
q.e: Without a committed lockfile and npm ci, each install can resolve different versions. npm ci installs exactly the lockfile and fails if it does not match package.json.

plain:
Semantic versioning gives version numbers a meaning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Patch (1.4.2) = bug fixes. Minor (1.5.0) = new features that do not break anything. Major (2.0.0) = breaking changes.

A lockfile records the exact versions you tested, so everyone and every server installs the same thing.
bridge: "react": "^18.2.0" in package.json means “any 18.x.x from 18.2.0 up, but not 19”. package-lock.json pins the exact one actually installed.

walk.title: Why CI broke when nobody changed code
steps: package.json says "some-lib": "^2.1.0". The repo has no committed lockfile (it was in .gitignore).
CI runs npm install. With no lockfile, npm resolves the newest version the range allows.
some-lib released 2.2.0 yesterday with an accidental breaking change. CI installs it and tests fail. Your laptop still has 2.1.0 in node_modules, so it works for you.
Fix: commit the lockfile and run npm ci in CI, which installs exactly what the lockfile says and fails if it is out of sync with package.json.
Then update deliberately: a bot (Renovate/Dependabot) opens a PR for 2.2.0, CI tests it, and you merge only if green.

terms: Allow updates that keep the left-most non-zero number: minor and patch for 1.x and above, only patch for 0.x.
Allow patch updates only (when a minor is given).
The exact resolved versions of every dependency.
Clean install exactly from the lockfile; deletes node_modules first and errors if the lockfile is out of sync.
insights: A range in package.json is a wish; the lockfile is the fact. Review lockfile changes in PRs, because that is what really changes.
Update dependencies a little every week. Updating two years at once becomes a project.
Read the changelog before major upgrades; it lists the breaking changes.

prod.summary: In production teams, dependency management is a weekly routine, not a yearly project: a committed lockfile, frozen installs in CI and Docker, and a bot that opens small, grouped update PRs. Seniors also treat new versions as a supply-chain risk: freshly published packages are the most likely to be malicious or broken.
checklist: The lockfile is committed, and CI and Dockerfiles use npm ci (or pnpm install --frozen-lockfile).
Renovate or Dependabot opens grouped PRs on a schedule; patch/minor updates of dev tools may auto-merge if CI is green.
New versions wait a few days before being adopted (Renovate minimumReleaseAge), so yanked or malicious releases are caught by others first.
Major upgrades are separate PRs, with the changelog or migration guide read and linked.
Dependencies on 0.x packages are pinned or reviewed more carefully, since minor bumps may break.
If you publish a package: breaking changes bump MAJOR, and an accidental break is fixed with a new release that restores compatibility.
npm audit or an equivalent runs in CI, with a clear rule for which severities block a merge.
numbers: SemVer 2.0.0: a pre-release has lower precedence than the release: 1.0.0-alpha < 1.0.0.
npm ci removes an existing node_modules and never writes to package.json or the lockfile.
failures: CI: npm error `npm ci` can only install packages when your package.json and package-lock.json are in sync.
A dependency was added or changed without committing the updated lockfile. Fix: run npm install locally and commit both files.
A ^0.4.0 dependency never updates past 0.4.x, and the team thinks Renovate is broken.
Caret on 0.x only allows patch updates. A move to 0.5.0 is treated as potentially breaking and needs a range change. Renovate opens it as a separate update.
After a two-year gap, upgrading the framework touches 400 files and takes a month.
Updates were postponed until many majors piled up. Fix: weekly grouped updates and one major at a time, while the gap is small.
A Docker build in production pulls a different transitive version than CI tested.
The Dockerfile runs npm install or copies package.json without the lockfile. Fix: COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ then RUN npm ci.

qs.s: package.json has "tiny-parser": "^0.3.1". The author publishes 0.3.4 and 0.4.0. Which version does a fresh install without a lockfile get?
o: 0.4.0, because caret allows minor updates
0.3.4, because for 0.x the caret allows only patch updates
0.3.1, because caret pins the exact version
1.0.0 when it is released
qs.e: Caret keeps the left-most non-zero number. In 0.3.1 that is the 3, so the range is >=0.3.1 <0.4.0.

qs.s: You maintain an internal library at 4.2.0. You rename an exported function and keep the old name as a deprecated alias that still works. Which version should you release?
o: 5.0.0, because a rename is always breaking
4.2.1, because it is small
4.3.0-beta, because it is deprecated
4.3.0, because nothing breaks for existing users and the new name is a new feature
qs.e: With the alias, old code still works, so it is backward compatible: MINOR. Removing the alias later is the breaking change and needs 5.0.0.

qs.s: A popular package is hijacked and a malicious patch release is published. It is removed from npm 6 hours later. Your Renovate config has minimumReleaseAge: "3 days" and CI uses npm ci. Were you exposed?
o: Yes, because npm ci always fetches the newest patch
Yes, because caret ranges allow patches
Very unlikely: the lockfile pins the old version and Renovate would not propose the new one before 3 days
No, because npm scans all packages before publishing
qs.e: npm ci follows the lockfile, not the range. The release age delay keeps the update PR from being opened during the window. A new npm install on a laptop without a lockfile could still pull it.

qs.s: npm audit reports a critical issue in minimist@1.2.5. It comes from old-cli@2.0.0, which pins "minimist": "1.2.5" exactly and has no newer release. The fixed version is 1.2.8. Which change is correct?

code.title: package.json

o: It does nothing: npm always respects a dependency's exact pin
Run npm audit fix --force, which is always safe
Add minimist as a direct dependency; npm then uses it for old-cli too
The overrides block shown forces 1.2.8 everywhere in the tree; then run tests, because old-cli was never tested with it
qs.e: overrides (npm 8.3+) replaces a version anywhere in the tree. A direct dependency does not change what old-cli resolves when its pin does not match. audit fix --force may install breaking majors. Long-term: replace or fork the unmaintained package.

qs.s: After adding a chart library, the app crashes with “Invalid hook call”. Read the output. What is the cause?

code.title: npm ls react
code.src:
app@1.0.0
├─┬ old-charts@3.1.0
│ └── react@18.3.1
├─┬ react-dom@19.2.0
│ └── react@19.2.0 deduped
└── react@19.2.0

o: React 19 removed hooks
Two copies of React are loaded: old-charts lists React as a normal dependency instead of a peerDependency, so its components use a different React than the app
react-dom is the wrong version
The lockfile is corrupt
qs.e: Hooks need exactly one React instance. Libraries that plug into the host framework must declare it in peerDependencies so the app's copy is used. Fix: upgrade to a version with React as a peer dependency (or that supports React 19), or force one copy with overrides if it is compatible.

qs.s: Consumers depend on "your-lib": "^2.4.0". You publish 2.5.0-beta.1 to try a new API. Do consumers get it on a fresh install without a lockfile?
o: Yes, because 2.5.0-beta.1 is greater than 2.4.0
Yes, but only with npm ci
No: a range only matches pre-releases when one of its comparators has a pre-release on the same MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, so ^2.4.0 skips it
No, because pre-releases cannot be published to npm
qs.e: node-semver excludes pre-releases from normal ranges on purpose, so people opt in. Also publish betas with a dist-tag (npm publish --tag beta) so npm install your-lib without a range keeps getting the stable latest.

qs.s: You maintain a public npm library. The next release drops support for Node 18 (you set "engines": { "node": ">=20" } and use an API only in Node 20). No exported function changes. Which version bump?
o: MAJOR: users on Node 18 can no longer use it, so it is breaking for them
PATCH: no API changed
MINOR: it only adds requirements
None: engines is ignored by npm
qs.e: Breaking means existing users' working setups stop working after an update their range allows. A ^ range would pull it into Node 18 projects and fail at runtime. The common convention (Node.js ecosystem, most major libraries) is that dropping a runtime version is a MAJOR change.

interview.q: How do you keep dependencies up to date in a large codebase without breaking production?
answer: Committed lockfile, frozen installs in CI and Docker (npm ci), so every install is the tested tree.
Renovate or Dependabot on a schedule, grouping low-risk updates; auto-merge only dev tools and patch/minor updates with good test coverage.
A release-age delay (for example 3 days) to avoid broken or malicious new versions.
Majors one at a time in their own PRs, with the changelog read; track how many majors behind you are.
Security updates fast-tracked; npm audit with a clear severity policy, and overrides for stuck transitive dependencies.

interview.q: Explain semantic versioning to a junior and tell me where it fails in practice.
answer: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking change, compatible feature, compatible fix. ^ allows minor and patch (only patch below 1.0), ~ allows patch.
It is a promise by humans: accidental breaking changes in minors happen, and what counts as “breaking” is not always clear (behaviour, types, runtime support).
0.x means anything may change; many packages stay there for years.
TypeScript types add another surface: a stricter type can break your build in a minor release.
So the real safety is lockfiles plus CI on update PRs, not the version number.

interview.q: How do you protect a project from supply-chain attacks through npm dependencies?
answer: Lockfile with integrity hashes and npm ci; no floating installs in CI or production builds.
Delay adoption of new versions (Renovate minimumReleaseAge), so most hijacked releases are removed before you see them.
Limit install scripts (for example --ignore-scripts where possible, or allow-lists in pnpm), since many attacks run in postinstall.
Review new dependencies: maintainers, download trend, size, whether you really need it.
Least-privilege CI tokens and no long-lived publish tokens, so a compromised build cannot publish or deploy; for your own packages, publish with provenance or trusted publishing.
